translation: The most important event for me in the winter of 1993 was my father returning, only a week before my mother's wedding.
One afternoon in December, he came to find me at school.
I ran all the way to the main gate, and from afar through a metal railings, saw him outside smoking.
He was wearing a long black coat, its collar turned up and covering half his face.
I couldn't make out his appearance clearly for some reason, but had an instinctive feeling that he wasn't doing too well.
My heart ached at this thought and tears welled up in my eyes.
I never imagined that my mother would contemplate remarrying.
Perhaps subconsciously, I felt she should continue to grieve over my father's departure, just like I did.
Besides, I thought she lacked the ability to find happiness again.
While there might be some truth to this, happiness seemed capable of finding her.
After all, as a beautiful woman, she didn't need to strive too much; she didn't have anything to do but just stand still.
I still remember, the winter that year was especially long, halfway through April and the spring blossoms had yet to bloom.
The news of our parent's divorce took a heavy toll on your spirits.
We hadn't had any new games to play in a while, so come dusk we would sit listlessly atop the death tower.
Among the body parts scattered about in our yard were several more arms added.
We used hooks to gather them all together, arranging them into the shape of a thousand-armed Bodhisattva.
In fact, my father didn't know anything about conducting business.
He just went to seek refuge with a cousin whom he didn't know very well.
My grandmother had a younger sister who moved to Beijing many years ago, later got married and gave birth there.
This cousin was her firstborn son who had always been considered an outcast in the entire family.
Just now, you said that everyone has a time when their fate is decided, as if life had suddenly been reined in.
Mine was probably at the age of eight.
That autumn, my father left Jinan and went to Beijing alone.
After that, I never had a home again.
I had no plans to keep the appointment.
Whatever the reasons, I believed there was no longer any necessity for us to meet again.
I sat on the couch, smoking one cigarette after another as it grew darker and darker outside, when suddenly there was a knock at the door.
The water delivery boy stood in the doorway holding a bucket, saying he'd just delivered water to a family in the western suburbs.
He wore a dirty grey woolen cap and his expression was blank.
Our conversation was difficult.
Each time it fell into silence, I felt a pressure on my heart and just wanted to end the meeting as soon as possible.
It seemed like you noticed this but continued to strive in finding a topic to discuss.
When the tea cooled down and the white fog inside the room had dispersed, you finally stood up and said goodbye.
When I closed the door, feeling relieved at last—that same instant—the doorbell rang again.
You were standing at the doorstep, asking me to come by Xiaobai Mansion later in the evening.
Before I could even decline your invitation, you had already walked through the apartment block's doors.
I walked into the kitchen and turned off the stove.
Half of the water in the kettle had already evaporated, filling the entire room with a white fog.
You sat down restlessly and watched me pour tea.
"Are you still living with your grandma and aunt?" you asked me.
I told you that my grandma had passed away, now it is just me living with my aunt.
"She never got married," you asked.
"Yes," I replied.

The white breath you exhale, the curly hair whipped up by the wind, the slight trembling of your knees under your coat these all convince me that you are a real presence before me rather than a continuation of an earlier dream.
It's been 18 years; it's not surprising that I couldn't recognize you.
You were without makeup and your pale face was slightly swollen.
Still, as they hoped, you turned out to be a beauty.
That peach-heart shaped face though looked gloomy–a look from staying in the big city for too long.
You asked me if I looked different from how you imagined me to be I just smiled ambiguously in response.
Honestly speaking, I have never imagined what you might look like when grown up.
For me, everything related to you has already been filed away and sealed with wax .
It might sound hurtful but truthfully speaking,I had never really hoped for a reunion with you.
I opened my eyes.
You were standing in the doorway.
I didn't know how long you had been there; you might have even seen me laughing in my sleep, and the sadness when I woke up, the weakest moments will surely be exposed to you.
Cheng Gong, you whispered my name in a hoarse voice as if you'd not spoken for a long time.
It was about to snow, and it was heavily overcast outside while it was pitch black inside our house.
The water on the stove boiled and bubbled.

I stared at you intently for a while, certain that I did not recognize you at all but suddenly felt deep connection with this stranger standing opposite to me under dim light which gave me chills down my spine recounting every stranded fragment of memories flipping swiftly in mind's box of pictures.
Then said "I am Li Jiaqi''.
